title: Masorti worldwide
hook: Masorti communities in Israel, Europe and Latin America

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was egalitarian: the woman in the second row, and the voice at the door saying ten. Did you notice who was counted in a room you walked into? Today, the same movement, far from where it began. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-four.

Friday evening in Buenos Aires. The street is loud, the synagogue is louder. Families crowd in, kids slide along the benches, someone is already humming the tune before the cantor starts. The prayers are in Hebrew, the same words said in Jerusalem and London tonight. But the rabbi's welcome is in Spanish, and the jokes during the announcements are in Spanish too. Afterward, out on the sidewalk, people say Shabbat shalom and then switch to arguing about football. Nobody here calls their synagogue Conservative. They use another word, the one you met three days ago.
screen: `FRIDAY NIGHT, BUENOS AIRES.` → `HEBREW PRAYERS, SPANISH WELCOME.` → `NOT CONSERVATIVE. MASORTI.`

segments.voice: Masorti worldwide. Masorti is Hebrew for traditional, and outside North America it is the name this movement goes by. The approach is the one you have been learning: halakha as binding, and halakha that develops, with rabbis reasoning from the sources and congregations choosing among approved answers. Now take it on a short trip. First, Latin America. In Buenos Aires there is a rabbinical seminary that trains rabbis to teach and lead in Spanish and Portuguese, so a Masorti community in South America can be led by someone who grew up in its own language. Second, Israel. There, the official rabbinate is Orthodox, and Masorti congregations build their life alongside it: their own synagogues, their own schools, their own rabbis, often trained in Jerusalem. Masorti in Israel means keeping tradition in Hebrew, at home, while asking for a place in the public square. Third, Europe. In Britain and on the continent there are Masorti synagogues, some large, some small enough that everyone knows who brought the cake. Each one sounds like where it is. Accents differ, tunes differ, the food after services differs. What travels is the method: take the law seriously, and let it develop. A psalm says it in one line: "O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth." All the earth, in many accents. One way of living the tradition, carried into many languages.
screen: `MASORTI MEANS TRADITIONAL.` · `LATIN AMERICA: RABBIS IN SPANISH.` · `ISRAEL: ALONGSIDE AN ORTHODOX RABBINATE.` · `EUROPE: EACH SOUNDS LIKE WHERE IT IS.` · then, large: `SING UNTO THE LORD, ALL THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn about one Masorti community. Settle, and breathe. Choose one of the three places: Buenos Aires, Jerusalem, or a small synagogue somewhere in Europe. Let it come into focus. The language on the street outside. The tune of a prayer you might already know, in a new accent. The people lingering after the service. Hold that one community in mind and wish it well, in whatever way you wish people well. Later today, if you're curious, look up one real Masorti synagogue and read its welcome page. The bell holds the time.
Masorti worldwide. The name Conservative Judaism goes by outside North America: one approach to the law, lived in Hebrew, Spanish, Portuguese and many other languages. Today's word.

Your line: worldwide. Today, when you do something ordinary, a meal, a greeting, a song, think of someone doing the same thing in another language, at the same hour. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-four.

notes: Institutions are described, not named: a rabbinical seminary in Buenos Aires (Seminario Rabínico Latinoamericano), rabbinical training in Jerusalem (Schechter), Masorti synagogues in Britain and continental Europe. Confirm each description is current and fair.
'Outside North America it is the name this movement goes by': confirm; some communities outside North America may still use 'Conservative'.
Israel: 'the official rabbinate is Orthodox, and Masorti congregations build their life alongside it' and 'asking for a place in the public square': confirm this is fair and not polemical.
Trapdoor floor 3 links masorti to masoret (tradition); confirm the derivation.
Hook scene in Buenos Aires is illustrative (Spanish welcome, Hebrew prayers); no specific congregation is meant.
